mean-median-mode.why: Three different answers to 'what is typical'. The mean uses every value and is dragged by extremes; the median is the middle and ignores how extreme the extremes are; the mode is the most common. Which one is honest depends on the shape of the data.
traps: Sort the data before taking a median. The median of an unsorted list is meaningless.

mean-reverse.why: Working backwards from an average means reasoning through the total: a mean of 80 over five tests requires 400 marks. Means cannot be averaged with each other unless they cover the same number of items.
traps: Averaging two averages is usually wrong. 50% on a 10-mark test and 90% on a 90-mark test is not 70% overall.

data-displays.why: Each display answers a different question: bar charts compare categories, line graphs show change over time, histograms show distribution, box plots show spread and outliers, two-way tables show the relationship between two categorical variables.
traps: In a two-way table, read carefully whether a percentage is of the row, the column or the whole table. Those are three different numbers and the choice between them is how statistics gets spun.

outliers-spread.why: A single number never describes a data set; you need centre *and* spread. Outliers pull the mean and the range hard while barely moving the median — which is exactly why house prices and incomes are reported as medians.
traps: An outlier is not automatically a mistake to delete. Deciding to exclude a data point is a judgement that has to be stated, not hidden.
